bearings.paper_claim: Perceived Big Five of public figures is predictable from the name embedding alone: cross-validated r = .78 (extraversion) to .88 (openness) after attenuation correction, raw .70-.80, N = 226 figures, 20-fold CV ridge on GPT-3 name embeddings; accuracy higher for more popular figures (r = .16 with log Wikipedia page views).
bearings.paper_location: Abstract; Results p.2-3 (Figure 1 green bars); Methods p.2 (CV, attenuation); Results p.3 (popularity r = .16)
bearings.system_side: fec/members/big5_llm.py de-identifies name parts, titles, party words and 50 state names before item scoring (deidentify, lines 196-204). The module docstring (lines 11-14) cites Cao and Kosinski as the reason, but gives the venue as PNAS Nexus 2024 and r = .76-.87, which match neither the paper's venue nor its figures.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper uses GPT-3 name embeddings and lay ratings of globally famous figures, not a chat model reading congressional text. Transfer to the Pink reader is by analogy and untested.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers, popularity r and page locations verified against the text. Softened only because the code docstring has the wrong venue and r values, and the 'reputational prior' wording is the analyst's, not the paper's.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper uses name embeddings only. It does not test whether removing names from surrounding text removes the signal. It notes predictions reflect only the period in the training data, and that extension to people absent from training data is untested.
bearings.paper_location: Discussion p.6 (lines 624-635); the paper has no separate Limitations heading
bearings.system_side: deidentify (big5_llm.py lines 196-204) blanks name parts longer than 2 characters, a fixed title list, party words and 50 state names, within 1,200-word chunks (CHUNK_WORDS = 1200 at line 51). Committee names, district cities and bill names are not removed. The --named probe (line 172, 30 members) is coded, but data/members holds only big5_llm_opus.json and big5_llm_sonnet.json plus caches, with no _named artifact. Name-part matching is case-insensitive, so common-word surnames also blank ordinary text.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Matters only where Pink scores feed a validity claim. The de-identification rationale is the code docstring's, not the paper's; the paper discusses a privacy threat from extracting traits from data (Discussion p.6), not text de-identification. The rel's Pink display-only status and the +.064 diagonal figure were not found in the brain concepts folder and remain unverified.
bearings.verifier_note: Code claims verified at the cited lines and in the data folder listing. Softened because the paper is not the motivation for de-identifying text as the summary states. The paper's relevant passage is Discussion p.6, not a Limitations section.

bearings.paper_claim: Controlling for likability plus birth year and gender lowers accuracy from corrected r = .78-.88 to r = .53-.70 (raw .43-.61). The paper attributes the likability-trait links to the personality halo effect and reports that the least likable figures sit at undesirable extremes of several traits.
bearings.paper_location: Results p.4 (lines 280-294), Figure 1 red bars; Table 2 p.4; halo discussion p.4 and p.5-6
bearings.system_side: big5_ctcm.py (lines 8-9) puts an orthogonal PINK METHOD factor over the five Pink indicators to absorb judge halo. big5_ctcm2.py (lines 3-8) repeats this with the embedding Blue as third indicator. The ct_p2 function in big5_improvements_eval.py (around line 223) removes the first principal component as the general evaluative factor. The paper contains no method factor and no single-factor model; the consistency with the CT-CM design is the analyst's inference.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's halo is in lay perceptions of famous people, with likability measured per figure. The rel says Melange has no per-member likability covariate; that was not checked here. The method factor is identified only by model structure, so the evidence bears on the halo's shape, not its size in congressional text.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers and the Results p.4 location verified. The paper's halo is a likability and demographics link, not a method factor, so the 'consistent with' sentence is inference. The ct_p2 PC1 removal is verified in code. The P2 MISS outcome was not verified: brain line 35 mentions P2 only in passing.

bearings.paper_claim: Perceptions of public figures track likability and demographics: birth year with extraversion, human r = .35 and model r = .44; women are perceived as more agreeable; an individual rater agrees with the aggregate at r = .56-.66.
bearings.paper_location: Results p.3 (lines 115-116); Results p.4 (lines 267-276, 272-273); Table 2 p.4
bearings.system_side: The brain file (single-look-holdout-discipline-case-1-moneyball-gate2.md, line 35) states A-ES is about .44 population-real (RKH benchmark .443 House, .393 Senate) plus about .21 text-tone halo. That line does not mention gold panels, expert or insider ratings, k=1 insiders or rater independence. The code_ref big5_improvements_eval.py:10 is a --p1 docstring line and does not discuss gold panels. The RKH benchmark appears to be the Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh text measure, not a rater panel.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's raters are lay Prolific workers rating world figures they recognise, not Hill insiders. The halo's size in Hill expert panels is untested by this paper. The gold-panel component is affected only if its raters use reputation and likability.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers and page locations verified. Softened because the system side is not supported at the cited locations: line 35 supports the .44 and .21 decomposition but not the gold-panel independence or k=1 insider assumptions, and the code citation is a CLI docstring line. Gold-panel rater counts were not confirmed.

related.why: Expert evaluations of senators' traits (Personality on the Hill) are a perception measure of public figures, the construct Cao and Kosinski predict from names, so reputation and halo can enter both. Cao does not cite it; the link is the analyst's.

LLM prompting for politicians' agency and communion from text. The coarse 3-point, cannot-tell-as-zero design in big5_llm.py cites Birkenmaier and Lechner. Cao does not cite it; the link is by topic and by that code citation.
Text-based measurement of elite Big Five from floor speech (Ramey, Klingler, Hollibaugh). Cao does not cite it. It marks the text route that a reputation prior must be kept separate from.

Meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations, which are mostly small. Cao does not cite it, and it measures a different target (self and observer reports from text), so the rel's comparison of Cao's r with LIWC effects is not like for like.

Meta-analysis of Big Five prediction from digital footprints. Cao's about r = .40 language benchmark is cited to Park et al. 2015 (ref 39), not to this meta-analysis, so the same-method label is not supported.

Review of personality computing that lists data privacy among its threats. Cao's privacy framing (Discussion p.6) rests on Kosinski's work instead, so the two are complementary rather than sources for each other.

Politicians' Big Five personality predicts national media coverage. Cao does not test popularity against it. The perceived-personality-drives-visibility gloss is the analyst's; the excerpt read does not establish that the traits are perceived.

summary_issues: Code citation mismatch: big5_llm.py line 12 cites Cao and Kosinski as PNAS Nexus 2024 with r = .76-.87. The paper is Scientific Reports 14:6735, with corrected r = .78-.88 and raw .70-.80. The summary flags this correctly; the code docstring needs fixing.

The summary says the paper is the cited motivation for de-identifying text. The paper does not discuss de-identifying text. The motivation comes from the code docstring; the paper's privacy argument concerns extracting traits from digital data (Discussion p.6).
The summary's statement that a large evaluative factor fits the CT-CM design is inference. The paper models no method or halo factor.

The summary's statement that the paper shows the prior lives in the name token overstates it. The paper shows name-embedding prediction of perceived traits, not that the signal is a reputational prior.
The summary's gold-panel link cites the brain file for k=1 insiders and independence, but line 35 of that file does not mention gold panels. The gold-panel link is unverified.
